title: Nasogastric tube insertion and checking its position

guidelineVersions: NHS Improvement NG tube resource set (July 2016)

related.why: Why he needs the tube, and the Gastrografin that will go down it
Another bedside procedure with consent and documentation

brief.setting: Surgical ward, on a nasogastric tube manikin
brief.scenario: Mr Raymond Kerr, 72, has adhesional small bowel obstruction on CT. He is vomiting and nil by mouth. The registrar has asked you to pass a nasogastric tube for decompression on free drainage; Gastrografin is planned through it later. He has capacity. A radio-opaque tube with length markings, lubricant, a 60 ml enteral syringe, CE-marked pH strips and a drainage bag are provided.
brief.task: Insert the nasogastric tube on the manikin, talking the examiner through each step, and explain how you would confirm its position.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Consent, cautions, measure, pass gently, then prove it's in the stomach before anything goes down it.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Flushing it or using the whoosh test because "it's only for drainage".
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'll explain the procedure, agree a stop signal and ask about head injury or oesophageal problems."

grid.label: Explanation and consent
grid.fail: Starts without explaining or agreeing a signal to stop.
grid.pass: Explains why and what it feels like; gains consent; agrees a signal to stop, such as raising a hand.
grid.high: Adds that the tube will ease his vomiting, and that nothing goes down it until its position is confirmed.

grid.label: Contraindications and cautions
grid.fail: Doesn't ask about head injury, oesophageal problems or previous surgery.
grid.pass: Asks about basal skull fracture, facial injury, oesophageal surgery, stricture or pouch, and varices.
grid.high: States that with altered anatomy or a basal skull fracture, he'd get senior help and have it placed under fluoroscopy.

grid.label: Equipment and measurement
grid.fail: Uses a tube without length markings, or doesn't measure.
grid.pass: Radio-opaque tube with length markings; CE-marked pH strips; measures nose to earlobe to xiphisternum and notes the mark.
grid.high: Knows the NEX length is an estimate; the tube may need adjusting by up to 10 cm to obtain aspirate.

grid.label: Insertion technique
grid.fail: Forces the tube against resistance, or carries on while he coughs.
grid.borderline: Passes the tube gently but never checks the mouth for coiling.
grid.pass: Sits him upright; lubricates; passes it horizontally, head not extended; dry swallows; stops and pulls back if he coughs or it resists.
grid.high: Uses a chin tuck; checks the mouth for coiling; stops after 3 attempts and asks for senior help.

grid.label: First-line check: pH (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Flushes the tube or puts anything down it before confirming position.
grid.pass: Aspirates; tests with CE-marked strips; pH 1 to 5.5 is the safe range; documents each result; nothing goes down until confirmed.
grid.high: Gets a second competent person to check readings between 5 and 6; knows acid suppression can push pH above 5.5.

grid.label: Unsafe checks (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Uses the whoosh test, litmus paper or the look of the aspirate.
grid.pass: States that the whoosh test, litmus, aspirate appearance and lack of respiratory distress never confirm position.
grid.high: Explains why: the lung and stomach are too close to locate a sound, and a tube in the lung may cause no symptoms.

grid.label: Second line: chest X-ray
grid.fail: Reads the tip alone, on an old film, or asks someone untrained.
grid.pass: X-ray if no aspirate or pH above 5.5; request states the purpose; read by someone trained; a tube in the lung comes out at once.
grid.high: Checks it's the latest film for this patient; four criteria: follows the oesophagus, bisects the carina, crosses the diaphragm midline, tip below left hemidiaphragm.

grid.label: Securing, drainage and documentation
grid.fail: Leaves it unsecured and records nothing.
grid.pass: Secures it; connects a drainage bag; records tube type, size and length at the nostril, and the pH or X-ray result.
grid.high: Makes clear the Gastrografin waits until position is confirmed and recorded; rechecks after vomiting or if the tube looks longer.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Picks up the tube.] Just going to pop this down, Mr Kerr.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Doesn't ask about head injury, previous surgery or swallowing.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Uses an unmarked tube and doesn't measure.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Pushes on while he coughs and gags.]

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Nothing's coming back. I'll flush 20 ml of water to free it up.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: [Injects air and listens over the stomach.] Good whoosh; it's in.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'll get an X-ray. The tip's below the diaphragm on this film, so it's fine. [Looks at yesterday's film.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Mr Kerr, I'd like to pass a tube through your nose into your stomach to drain it and ease the vomiting. It's uncomfortable but quick. Is that OK? Raise your hand if you want me to stop.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Have you had a head or facial injury, surgery on your gullet, a narrowing or pouch, or varices?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Radio-opaque tube with length markings; CE-marked strips.] Nose to earlobe to xiphisternum: 55 cm.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Sits him upright, lubricates, passes it horizontally with his head neutral.] Swallow for me. [He coughs; pulls back slightly and waits, then advances to the mark.]

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Aspirates with the 60 ml syringe, tests with a CE-marked strip.] pH 1 to 5.5 would be safe. It's 6.5, so it's not confirmed; I'll document it, and nothing goes down.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I won't use the whoosh test, litmus or the look of the aspirate; none of them confirm position, and nor does him being comfortable.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Chest X-ray, stating it's to check NG position, read by someone trained. If it's in the lung, it comes straight out.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: [Tapes it, connects a drainage bag.] I'll record the tube type, size, 55 cm at the nostril, and the pH and X-ray result.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Mr Kerr, this tube will drain your stomach and should stop the vomiting. You may gag briefly. Raise your hand to stop me. Nothing goes down it until we've proved where it is. Happy to go ahead?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Any head or facial injury, gullet surgery, narrowing, pouch or varices? With any of those, or a skull base fracture, I'd get senior help and have it placed under X-ray screening.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Checks markings.] NEX is 55 cm, but that's an estimate; I may need to adjust by up to 10 cm to get aspirate.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Upright, head neutral, horizontal along the nose; chin tuck and dry swallows as he's nil by mouth; pauses when he coughs; opens his mouth to check it hasn't coiled.] If I can't pass it in 3 attempts, I'll stop and call my registrar.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Aspirates bile-stained fluid.] pH 6.5. He's on omeprazole, which can raise it, and bile doesn't prove anything. Outside 1 to 5.5, so not confirmed. Between 5 and 6, I'd get a second check.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: No whoosh test: the lung and stomach are too close to tell where a sound comes from. And a tube in the lung can cause no symptoms at all.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: X-ray requested to confirm NG position. [Checks it's today's film for Mr Kerr.] It follows the oesophagus, bisects the carina, crosses the diaphragm in the midline, and the tip is below the left hemidiaphragm.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: [Tapes to the cheek, free drainage.] I'll document the four criteria and that it's safe to use; the Gastrografin waits until that's recorded. Any vomiting or if it looks longer, recheck before use.

failures.move: Flushing water or giving Gastrografin before position is confirmed.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: fluid into the lung. A misplaced tube not detected before a flush or medication is a Never Event.

failures.move: Relying on the whoosh test or the appearance of the aspirate.
failures.consequence: Safety-critical: these cannot tell lung from stomach.

failures.move: Reading an old film, or judging the tip position alone.
failures.consequence: X-ray misinterpretation has been the main cause of harm from misplaced tubes.

failures.move: Blind insertion after a basal skull fracture or with a pharyngeal pouch.
failures.consequence: Risk of intracranial or oesophageal placement; needs senior help and fluoroscopy.

recovery.when: He coughs violently as the tube passes
recovery.line: I'll pull back a little and wait. Tell me when you're ready, and we'll try again with a swallow.
Actually, that isn't a safe check. I'll use pH, and an X-ray if that doesn't confirm it.

knowledge.fact: pH testing is first line, with 1 to 5.5 the safe range; X-ray is second line. Nothing goes down the tube until position is confirmed.
Never Event: a naso- or oro-gastric tube in the pleura or respiratory tract, not detected before a feed, flush or medication.
The four X-ray criteria: follows the oesophagus, bisects the carina or bronchi, crosses the diaphragm in the midline, tip below the left hemidiaphragm.
After its 2024 consultation, NHS England is exploring a new approach to the Never Events framework.

The 2016 alert and resource set cover feeding tubes and exclude wide-bore drainage (Ryle's) tubes, but the Never Event covers a feed, flush or medication through any misplaced NG tube, so confirm position before Gastrografin.

recall.think: Lung or stomach? Prove it before anything goes down.
recall.say: "pH 1 to 5.5, or an X-ray read with the four criteria."
do: pH, then X-ray; document before use
recall.finish: Secured, draining, position documented before Gastrografin.

sources.name: National Patient Safety Agency: Patient Safety Alert NPSA/2011/PSA002: Reducing the harm caused by misplaced nasogastric feeding tubes in adults, children and infants, with Supporting Information
sources.supports: 'Feeding' includes the introduction of any feed, liquid or medication; tubes radio-opaque throughout with visible length markings (c); pH paper CE marked for human gastric aspirate (d); nothing flushed or introduced until the tip is confirmed in the stomach by pH or X-ray (e); pH testing first line, with pH 1 to 5.5 the safe range, each result documented (f); a second competent person checks readings between pH 5 and 6; patients on acid-suppressing medication more often have pH 6 or above; X-ray second line only, with the request stating its purpose, the latest film for the correct patient, interpretation by someone competent, and any tube in the lung removed immediately (g); whoosh tests, litmus paper and the appearance of aspirate never used (i); with altered anatomy (oesophageal fistula, pharyngeal pouch) or basal skull fracture, seek senior help and insert only under fluoroscopy; NEX measurement; record tube type, size and external length; recheck before use after vomiting, retching or coughing, or if displacement is suggested

sources.name: NHS Improvement: Resource set: Initial placement checks for nasogastric and orogastric tubes (supporting Patient Safety Alert NHS/PSA/RE/2016/006)
sources.supports: Covers fine-bore nasogastric and orogastric tubes used for feed, fluid or medication; wide-bore nasogastric (Ryle's) tubes used to drain the stomach, for example in intestinal obstruction, are outside its scope; checking tube placement before use by pH and, when necessary, X-ray is essential; do not use the whoosh or bubble test (the lungs and stomach are too close to locate sound); do not use blue litmus paper; absence of respiratory distress and appearance of aspirate are not indicators of position; pH 1 to 5.5 is the first-line test and the safe range must not be widened; stomach pH about 1-3 when empty and 4-5 after food; acid-reducing medication can give pH 6 or above; X-ray when aspirate in the safe range cannot be obtained; four criteria: the tube follows the oesophagus and avoids the contours of the bronchi, clearly bisects the carina or bronchi, crosses the diaphragm in the midline, and the tip is clearly visible below the left hemidiaphragm; record that the film viewed is the most current for the correct patient; unused tubes found in the lung removed immediately; 95 incidents including 32 deaths, September 2011 to March 2016, with X-ray misinterpretation the main error

sources.name: National Nurses Nutrition Group (BAPEN NG special interest group): Good practice guidance: Safe insertion and ongoing care of nasogastric (NG) feeding tubes in adults
sources.supports: Agree a signal to stop and a swallow as the tube passes the pharynx; sit upright, head supported; NEX measurement (nose, earlobe, xiphisternum) is only an estimate and the tube may need adjusting by up to 10 cm to obtain aspirate; insert aiming horizontally, not upwards; head not hyperextended; a chin tuck can help; a drink with a straw if safe to swallow, otherwise a dry swallow; if significant resistance, stop and pull back; if coughing, stop, pull back slightly and wait; check the mouth for coiling; never force; a maximum of 3 attempts, then senior help; secure ideally to the cheek; contraindications may include basal skull fracture, maxillofacial disorders, unstable cervical spine injury, oesophageal stricture, pouch, tumour or surgery, and bleeding varices (guidance for feeding tubes; gastric decompression tubes are outside its scope)

sources.name: NHS Improvement / NHS England: Never Events list 2018
sources.version: First published January 2018; last updated February 2021
sources.supports: Never Event 13, misplaced naso- or oro-gastric tubes: misplacement in the pleura or respiratory tract that is not detected before starting a feed, flush or medication administration; all settings providing NHS-funded care

sources.name: NHS England: Never Events framework: 2024 consultation findings
sources.supports: After the 2024 consultation, NHS England began a discovery phase to explore a new approach to the Never Events framework, testing alternatives with stakeholders; the existing framework remains in use meanwhile

media.task: Interpret the check film using the four criteria
media.description: Adult chest X-ray, anonymised, showing a radio-opaque nasogastric tube following the oesophagus, bisecting the carina, crossing the diaphragm in the midline with the tip clearly below the left hemidiaphragm

partner.opening: Please insert a nasogastric tube for Mr Kerr on this manikin, talking me through what you're doing.

reveals.finding: No head or facial injury, no oesophageal surgery, stricture, pouch or varices. Takes omeprazole 20 mg daily.
Say: "The NEX mark is at 55 cm."
Say: "He coughs as the tube reaches about 20 cm." If the candidate pulls back and waits, say: "It now passes easily to the mark."
Say: "You get 40 ml of green, bile-stained fluid. The pH strip reads 6.5."
Show the check film if available; otherwise ask: "What would you look for on the film?"

push.question: Why not use the whoosh test?
push.expect: The lung and stomach are too close to locate a sound; it cannot tell lung from stomach.

push.question: What pH confirms the tube is safe to use?
push.expect: pH 1 to 5.5 on CE-marked strips; second competent check if between 5 and 6.

push.question: What do you look for on the X-ray?
push.expect: Latest film, correct patient; follows the oesophagus, bisects the carina, crosses the diaphragm midline, tip below the left hemidiaphragm.

curveballs.prompt: The X-ray shows the tube in the right main bronchus.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Remove it immediately, document, and re-site with a new tube.

curveballs.prompt: The nurse wants to flush 20 ml of water "to get some aspirate".
curveballs.safeAnswer: No: nothing goes down until position is confirmed; it also contaminates the pH test.

curveballs.prompt: "It's only for drainage. Why check it at all?"
curveballs.safeAnswer: The national feeding-tube checks don't cover a drainage-only tube, but Gastrografin, medicines or a flush may go down it; a misplaced tube used for any of these is a Never Event, so confirm first.

curveballs.prompt: Next morning he has vomited and the tape is loose.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Recheck position with pH, or X-ray if needed, before anything goes down it.
